meta.title: "Have you stopped cheating yet?" — a question you can't answer honestly | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child to spot the hidden accusation inside a question and bring back reality: "I didn't do that". Game-based critical thinking course for children aged 10–16.

hero.headline: Is your child cornered by a question that makes them "guilty" already?
hero.subheadline: "Have you stopped cheating yet?" "Why did you do it again?" Whatever they answer, they look guilty. Your child gets flustered, makes excuses or goes silent — because the accusation is already hidden inside the question.

media.alt: A child cornered by a question where any answer is an admission of guilt

pain.title: It's not a question — it's a hidden accusation
pain.body:
The wording already hides an assumption that the child did something. "Have you stopped yet?" — both "yes" and "no" confirm they were doing it. There's no honest answer: the very form of the question leaves no way out.

This isn't "not knowing what to say" or freezing from shame. The child falls into a trap: the question sounds ordinary, so they start to answer it — and by doing so accept someone else's version of events as the starting point.

The result — the child defends and excuses themselves for something that never happened. They agree with the hidden accusation simply because they answered the question — and someone else's "version" becomes their truth about themselves.

solution.title: "Sila Slova" — a detective drama that teaches critical thinking
solution.body: 50 episodes, 13 critical thinking lessons. Your child plays — but is actually learning to protect themselves.
bullets: 🔍 Notices that the question already hides an accusation
🧠 Answers the substance, not the form — the assumption itself
💬 Stops the question and brings back reality: "I didn't do that", "that's not true"
🛡️ Doesn't accept someone else's "version of events" as the truth about themselves

social_proof.quote: "Why did you do it again?" used to send my son straight into excuses. Now he says first: "Wait, I didn't do that" — and won't let something that never happened be pinned on him.
social_proof.author: Kateryna, mum of 10-year-old Bohdan

faq.q: Is it a game or a learning course?
faq.a: Both at the same time. "Sila Slova" looks like a detective series, but every episode contains a hidden critical thinking lesson.

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
faq.a: Ideal for 10–16 year olds. At this age, children are receptive to new thinking patterns and are still forming their views.

faq.q: How much time is needed each day?
faq.a: 15–20 minutes per episode. Flexible schedule — your child can come back at any convenient time.

faq.q: Is registration required for the demo?
faq.a: No. The demo episode is fully open — no registration, no subscription, no personal data required.
